biography.text: Abū al-Qāsim al-Zahrāwī (Latinized as Albucasis) was an Andalusi physician associated with Córdoba. This batch studies one passage from the surgical treatise at the end of his *Kitāb al-Taṣrīf* and the history of its illustrated witnesses; it is not a complete biography.
gaps: Build a sourced biography from Arabic biographical witnesses and specialist scholarship; distinguish secure evidence from later honorifics and approximate dates.

timeline.text: The *Kitāb al-Taṣrīf* is generally dated to the late tenth or early eleventh century. The surgical treatise was translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in the twelfth century; surviving illustrated copies are later witnesses and should not be confused with the author's own manuscript.
gaps: Establish composition chronology and translation dates from the Arabic/Latin witnesses, colophons, and critical edition rather than adopting rounded dates from summaries.

fields.text: The passage examined here concerns surgical education and judgement: Hamarneh's published account of the treatise's preface reports four disastrous cases attributed to physicians operating without adequate anatomical and practical preparation. Hamarneh also compares illustrations in Arabic manuscript witnesses with later Latin and vernacular reproductions, noting that many later drawings were modified. These are claims mediated through a 1960s scholarly study and require collation with the 1973 Arabic-English edition and manuscript images.
gaps: Collate Hamarneh's translated preface passage with Spink and Lewis's 1973 Arabic-English critical edition and the manuscript witness used for its text.
Identify exact folios and compare the instrument drawing in BnF Arabe 2953 against a Latin witness before curating an image or assigning a particular instrument.
Research instruments and operative methods as separate investigations; do not import modern clinical interpretations or present historical procedures as medical advice.

legacy.text: The British Library catalogues a fourteenth-century illustrated Latin translation of the surgical treatise and records a colophon attributing translation from Arabic to Gerard of Cremona. Hamarneh discusses the Latin text's reception and illustration history, but this batch does not trace a specific procedure into a later author's work or establish priority for any instrument.
gaps: Trace transmission and influence with specific textual parallels, manuscript evidence, or citations; avoid broad claims of sole invention or 'father of surgery'.

sources.title: Drawings and Pharmacy in al-Zahrāwī's 10th-Century Surgical Treatise
sources.authorOrInstitution: Sami Khalaf Hamarneh, Smithsonian Institution, Museum of History and Technology, Bulletin 228, Paper 22 (1962), pp. 81–94
sources.notes: Full text consulted. At printed pp. 83–85 Hamarneh outlines the work and compares Arabic manuscript illustrations with later Latin/vernacular copies; at p. 87 he reports a translated account from the surgical preface about four fatal outcomes after unskilled operations and emphasizes anatomical and practical preparation. The source is a secondary study, not a direct reading of the Arabic passage; its own modern clinical/historical assessments are not adopted without corroboration.

investigations.title: Surgical training in the preface and the changing life of instrument drawings
investigations.field: History of medicine / surgery / manuscript illustration
investigations.historicalProblem: How does the surgical treatise present the risks of untrained operative practice, and what should historians account for when using later copies of its instrument illustrations?
investigations.historicalContext: The surgical treatise is the final section of al-Taṣrīf. Hamarneh's 1962 study reports a passage from its preface about four fatal outcomes and compares drawings in Arabic witnesses with later Latin/vernacular reproductions. The British Library catalogue documents one later Latin witness copied in fourteenth-century Italy; BnF Arabe 2953 is a digitized Arabic witness whose catalogue describes instrument illustrations. These witnesses belong to different moments in transmission and must not be treated as authorial originals without qualification.
investigations.method: This batch compares source descriptions rather than reconstructing an operation: Hamarneh's account of the preface and illustration comparisons is checked against institutional catalogue records for BnF Arabe 2953 and BL Add MS 36617, and against the BNF catalogue record for the 1973 critical edition. The named manuscript images and edition pages are queued for direct collation before any individual instrument or procedure is asserted.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: Hamarneh states that the surgical section is the work's final treatise and reports four tragic outcomes in the preface associated with inadequate anatomy and operative skill. He notes that many drawings in later reproductions differ substantially from Arabic manuscript drawings. BL records coloured instrument drawings across ff. 1r–51r in its Latin copy and a colophon on f. 51r. BnF metadata identifies Arabe 2953 as the final treatise and says it contains instrument figures; these descriptions do not establish the exact appearance of a particular tool or folio.
investigations.reportedResult: The consulted evidence supports a careful, limited conclusion: the transmitted treatise's preface, as reported by Hamarneh, foregrounds anatomical knowledge and practical competence; instrument images have a copy and translation history in which later reproductions can depart from Arabic manuscript drawings. Exact text, image variants, and the author's own wording remain to be verified against the 1973 edition and digitized manuscript.
investigations.whatWasNew: No claim of the first surgical manual, a first instrument, or sole invention is made. This case documents the text's reported pedagogical framing and an image-transmission problem that affects how scientific illustrations should be presented.
investigations.limitations: The Arabic passage and manuscript page images were not directly inspected; Hamarneh is the intermediary for the preface claim and his article dates to 1962. BL Add MS 36617 digital images are listed as unavailable. BnF Arabe 2953 is linked to Gallica/IIIF but the image sequence was not retrieved in this pass. No surgical technique is reproduced as practical advice. The four cases are not independently corroborated here.
investigations.laterInfluence: The BL catalogue and Hamarneh describe Latin transmission and reception, but this investigation does not trace a specific preface passage or instrument design into a named later author. Such influence requires separate textual comparison.

Compare that Arabic image with one Latin witness illustration and document variants without assuming later copies preserve authorial drawings.
